01 / THE BRIEF

Make the purchase useful.
Then make it credible.

  • Working, earning consumers.
  • Active lifestyle. Beginners included.
  • Not children.
Aa

Brand voice

  • Short. Punchy. Playful.
  • A challenge, not a lecture.
  • Benefits before specifications.
  • Movement before motivation clichés.

RESEARCH / THE WIDER PAID-SOCIAL ASSIGNMENT

What the category does, and what it leaves open.

Before any concept, I read Cultstore's live ads in the Meta Ad Library and scanned the category's active ads in India.

Cultstore's own ads

The pattern to respect.

  • Hook: one line, one idea. A pain ("sore after leg day?") or an identity line.
  • No more than three concrete proofs: "no-drill", the load rating, "foam grip". Never "premium quality".
  • The ending: offer code, free delivery, Shop Now.
  • Carousels: emoji as bullets, sentence case, caps only for one word.
  • Massager video: pain question, relief claim, three features fast, then price and CTA.
How I studied them

The pattern, never a copy.

  • Live ads pulled from the Meta Ad Library, sorted by impressions.
  • The winning pattern: problem or benefit hook, product, two or three concrete features, exact offer, Shop Now.
  • Individual ads flagged as pattern references. The pattern, never a copy.
  • Prices and ratings taken from cultstore.com, and real customer reviews quoted verbatim.
The category's ads

What every doorway-bar brand says.

  • Doorway transformation, no-drill, exercise variety and space-saving are the shared language.
  • So none of them can be the unique claim.
  • Common formats: a short outcome hook on the first frame, a creator demo in a real home, 20 to 30 second videos, one benefit per ad, a simple Shop Now.
  • Adjacent equipment brands lead with clutter: a rack of dumbbells replaced by one set.
What worked

Carry these forward.

  • A short outcome hook on frame one.
  • A creator demo in a real home setting.
  • One clear benefit per ad.
  • A simple Shop Now.
What did not fit

Leave these out.

  • A family or kids angle: not the audience.
  • Price urgency alone: against a premium positioning.
  • A dry feature checklist alone: generic, and the swipe stops.
  • Generated scenes sold as proof, fake urgency, or calling an ad a winner without sales data.
In the Meta Ad Library

Cultstore's live ads.

What I did with it

The gap, and three decisions.

The open gap

Every pull-up ad from the brand was feature-led. The emotional "first pull-up" angle was empty.

Features support

The capacity checklist went into support lines, never the hero.

No comparison card

A "best bar" claim could not be defended. The load rating is not unique in the category and there was no independent testing. Positioned on value and features instead.

Concepts picked

The two least duplicated routes had a human angle no pull-up ad used yet.

Tested directions

Show equipment in a real home and routine. Open on one buyer goal, not everything at once: a published retailer test found interest-tailored video lifted ROAS 51% over generic. Keep refreshing real product demos.

My recommendation

A short real-home setup-and-use video: one objection, one real demo. Stronger to test than an exercise-list carousel.

02 / END-TO-END PROCESS

Study. Separate. Write.
Review. Tighten. Present.

01 / UNDERSTAND

Brief + product

  • Define the reader and short, playful voice.
  • Keep the pull-up bar central.
  • Separate the wider assignment from the two sets shown.
02 / RESEARCH

References + evidence

  • Study five supplied CultStore ad references.
  • Extract writing patterns, not performance claims.
  • Use customer quotes as the review route's evidence.
03 / EXPLORE

Hooks + routes

  • Start with five buying-angle routes.
  • Consolidate overlapping fit-into-life angles.
  • Develop library, goals, reviews and education sets.
04 / SELECT

Different buying jobs

  • Keep the exercise library for useful range.
  • Keep customer evidence for purchase doubts.
  • Do not pair two exercise catalogues.
05 / REFINE

Copy before polish

  • Reduce competing cover messages.
  • Test shorter drilling lines through review.
  • Fix grammar, highlights, arrows and spacing.
06 / DELIVER

Client + portfolio

  • Separate seven-card client sets from eight-card portfolio sets.
  • Keep the portfolio CTA out of the client document.
  • Present the creative. Do not invent results.
Brief→References→Routes→Selection→Review→Delivery

The sequence summarises the recorded work. It was iterative, not a pre-set six-step methodology.

What the loop actually changed

Concept checkThe goals set repeated the library. Change the job, not just the hook.
Line check"No excuses allowed" was the chosen endpoint after shorter alternatives.
Reading checkHighlight useful words. Remove decorative arrows when the line already carries the contrast.

Review choices are documented preferences and copy decisions, not A/B-test results.

03 / THE REFERENCE STUDY

Borrow the writing pattern.
Not the promise.

Reference writing → reader value
OUTCOME FIRSTDoorway → training

Lead with the activity, then explain the hardware.

RANGE AS VALUEOne product → many uses

Make variety visible without forcing an exact count.

FEATURE AS BENEFITLow mount → useful effort

Use wordplay only when the exercise scene explains it.

What did not carry acrossMassage-chair relaxation ≠ strength-training promise.Another product's rating ≠ this bar's proof.Visible ad ≠ proven winner.

Also studied: 4-in-1 home gym and massage chairs. The supplied library was sorted by impressions. That did not expose impression counts, clicks or sales for these reference ads.

05 / COPY DECISIONS

One route adds value.
The other removes doubt.

C1 / REFRAME THE PURCHASE

Bar → workout range

Mounting positions are not the benefit. The exercises they enable are.

So: position strip + exercise scene + named move. Not a spec list.

C2 / MAKE THE CLAIM ACCOUNTABLE

Brand says → customer says

A quote grounds the headline in one person's experience.

So: keep names and useful detail. Do not turn one review into a guarantee.

THE PAIR / AVOID DUPLICATION

Range + reassurance

Two exercise catalogues repeat value. Reviews add a missing reason to buy.

This was a creative decision. No analytics drove the selection.

FEATURE

Top / middle / low mount

→
READER BENEFIT

More ways to train

COPY PLAYBOOK / THE WORKING RULES

The rules every card followed.

Written down after round one, and carried into round two.

Working direction

A paid-ads copywriter's brief.

  • Written as a fitness paid-ads copywriter on Meta formats, conversion first.
  • Audience 25 to 35, active lifestyle, beginners included.
  • Short, punchy, quirky, motivating, challenging.
  • Research-backed, no over-claiming. User-centric claims over spec dumps.
  • Keywords gym-goers actually search.
Copy rules

Sharp, honest, one job a line.

  • The product is the hero on every card. An add-on earns a card only if it adds exercises on the bar, and only Cult Store SKUs.
  • One job per line. No two lines doing the same work.
  • Register is a spectrum: direct, funny, witty, satirical. Wordplay is never forced.
  • Every carousel is distinct, and the opener matches its own theme.
Claims

Real, or not at all.

  • Real published reviews, verbatim, with names and ratings.
  • Live prices and ratings from cultstore.com, so traffic goes to the brand store.
  • No medical or pain-relief claims. Framed as strength and benefit instead.
  • Product named exactly as on the store. Title Case for add-ons.
Client rules

Evergreen and brand-first.

  • No festive or seasonal elements.
  • No other marketplaces' logos or names. Only the brand's own store rating.
  • Implement what the client asked. Push back once with an alternative, then follow the client.
Design direction

Imagery directed card by card.

Same model, full photos

One model across a set, full-size uncut photos, and the brand's official colours.

Exercise-first images

Exercise names inside the image, with the targeted muscles as a soft glow, not circles.

Reviews as chats

Testimonials styled as real chat bubbles, with flat highlight bands on one to three key words.

A real CTA slide

The last card reads as a call to action, not another content card.

06 / DESIGN SUPPORTS THE COPY

Make the argument readable.
Do not decorate over it.

C1 / USEFULNESS HIERARCHY
Buying question
↓
Range promise + product
↓
Mounting position → exercise → benefit

The cover collage makes variety visible. Position strips give the next cards a clear entry point.

C2 / TRUST HIERARCHY
Challenge headline
↓
Quote + selected benefit words
↓
Name / rating + exercise scene

The headline invites attention. The quote supplies the evidence. Colour helps scanning; it does not create proof.

Keep

  • C1 collage and the bar as hero.
  • Names and useful review detail.
  • Black / coral / yellow CTA contrast.

Reduce

  • Two competing opener questions.
  • Marketplace logos and offer clutter on C2's hook.
  • Long highlights and excess CTA white space.

Separate

  • Copy and imagery direction from final brand production.
  • Portfolio offers from current prices.
  • Presentation mockups from media that ran.

These are layout and imagery decisions supporting the copy. Final design and media running belong to the brand.

07 / BEFORE AND AFTER

The strongest changes
removed competing jobs.

01
C1 / COVER

One objection. One range promise.

→

No time for gym?

Keep: "No room for a home gym?"

Time and space compete for the opener. Space leads directly into one compact bar's range.

"22 exercises" became "Endless exercises". The shorter selected set no longer centres an exact count.

The collage stayed. A text-only cover was a misread, not the chosen direction.

02
C2 / TRUST HOOK

Own the evidence. Lose the borrowed logos.

→

Before: "Big claims? We'd rather show receipts." + a buying question + marketplace ratings + an offer.

After: "The reviews are IN. / We have set the bar HIGH."

The first cover asked the reader to process four messages. The final cover points to one proof source: CultStore customer experience.

Festival and marketplace elements left the hook. The supplied portfolio CTA kept its festival offer.

Removal was not universal. The supplied warning-triangle asset also retained a faint stock watermark.

03
C2 / INSTALLATION

Keep the benefit. Tighten the challenge.

→

Before: "No drilling required, / so you better find a diff excuse!"

"No drilling. No excuses."↓ too short"No drilling required. No excuses."↓ final choice"No drilling required.
No excuses allowed."

"Required" preserves the practical benefit. "Allowed" makes the challenge firmer. The quote supplies the installation experience.

The final wording was Diya's explicit pick, not a performance winner.

04
PORTFOLIO ONLY / CTA

The line already shows the contrast.

→

Supplied original: "Pull yourself up. Bring the price down."

Diya's replacement: "Your turn to raise the bar, / While the prices are down."

Up/down arrows were requested, added, then removed. Aesthetic preference, not an analytics decision.

The final hierarchy carries the contrast: black bold / coral bold italic / yellow band. Full stop added. Excess white space tightened.

The supplied price tiers and festival badge stayed. The client document did not receive this portfolio CTA.

GRAMMAR, NOT A NEW CONCEPT
Radhika had will.→Radhika had a will.

One missing article. Name and wordplay stayed.

HIGHLIGHT MEANING, NOT SENTENCES
Long full-line runs→Selected benefit words

Speed, weight and stability became scanning anchors. Lighter pink restored readability. Importance came before colour.

ARCHIVED OFFER, DIFFERENT AUDIENCE
Client: 7 cards→Portfolio: 8 cards

C1's supplied DIY close stayed, with 12/12 changed to 8/8. C2 received the revised price close. Neither is a current shopping offer.

CLIENT ROUNDS / THE WORKING DOCUMENT

Twelve comments. All worked in.

The client reviewed both carousels on the working doc. Every comment was implemented and synced across the doc and the image folders.

Carousel 1 · 8 comments

Less crowded. More direct.

  • Cover: too crowded. Kept one question and two lines.
  • Cards 2 to 4: tags added, subheadings removed.
  • Card 5: reframed around versatility.
  • Card 7: reframed around progression.
  • Length: seven cards is right. Cards 8 to 12 removed.
Carousel 2 · 4 comments

Crisp. Evergreen. Brand-first.

  • Cover: one great hook. Festive elements and other platforms' logos removed, so ads can run all year and drive sales to the store.
  • Copy: trimmed so the review is the focus.
  • Length: one hook and six testimonials. One card removed.
  • Cover line: "Pssst, see what others have to say about it."
Why each change mattered

What the client was steering toward.

Fewer slides

The client wanted tighter carousels. Seven cards for the library, one hook and six testimonials for the reviews. Cards 8 to 12 and one testimonial came out.

Regular posting

The festival offer and dates were removed so the carousels work in regular posting, not only in a sale window.

More imaginable

A fixed exercise count would have capped the idea and needed more slides. "Endless" lets the viewer picture their own routine.

Bar first

The pull-up bar stays the hero. Add-ons stay only where they add exercises on the bar.

Harder moves

The cards climb in difficulty, ending on weighted hanging raises, instead of repeating beginner moves.

Brand store first

Other platforms' logos and ratings came out so every ad drives sales to the Cultstore itself.

Before → after

What the client's comments changed.

ROUND TWO / GUN MASSAGERS

Objections as slides.

01 / Briefing

The routine, not the recovery.

  • Angle: "Don't wait till you're Sore." Make muscle care part of the routine: before training, between workouts, after hard sessions.
  • Deliverables: carousel and video.
  • Marketed as a category. The price shown is "Starting from Rs 799", never a single model.
02 / Applying round one

Fewer words, first time right.

  • Less, uncongested copy: two lines per card, with image tags for the design team.
  • Concepts pitched as a blocker solved and what each slide shows.
  • Real claims only. Specs checked across models: one button, 4 heads, 6 speeds, Type-C.
03 / The carousel

Excuse Audit.

  • A hero, then one objection per card: does it even work, too complicated, too expensive, too bulky, no time, not for me.
  • Each card shows its own claim: a physio bills every visit, Cult bills you once. The remote has more buttons.
  • A Graphite theme, picked from white, cream and graphite options.
04 / The video

The Cult Routine.

  • Five scenes: an intro line, then before and after across gym and sport.
  • Before and after side by side with a vertical divider. Feature tags under each scene.
  • A vertical cut of about 28 seconds.

09 / ANALYTICS AND PROJECTIONS

What can be estimated.
What cannot.

OBSERVED / CULTSTORE

Creative, not returns.

The pull-up reference was active when checked. Its details showed the creative, platforms and a 22 September 2026 start date.

No spend, impression count, CTR, purchases or ROAS was displayed. No Ads Manager report was supplied for this project.

Reference checked 14 October ↗
COMPARABLE / NOT CULTSTORE

2.01% CTR

Sports & Outdoors median. Triple Whale: 40,000+ brands, August 2025-July 2026.

Mixed markets and formats. Not an India-only carousel result. Not a forecast for either creative.

Read the dataset ↗
CONDITIONAL PROJECTION / A SCENARIO, NOT A PROMISE

If 10,000 impressions achieved the 2.01% comparable CTR:

10,000impressions assumed×2.01%external benchmark=201clicks estimated

The same scenario applies to both routes. Assigning C2 a higher rate without a test would invent an uplift.

100 clicksat an assumed 1% CTR201 clicksat the 2.01% benchmark300 clicksat an assumed 3% CTR

The 1% and 3% values are sensitivity inputs, not sourced category benchmarks or confidence bounds. Click definition must match the source before comparison. Clicks are not landing-page visits or purchases.

Why no sales or ROAS forecast?

  • Spend and CPM are unknown.
  • India equipment data does not match the broad dataset.
  • Offer, page conversion and order value are unknown.
  • Attribution window and click definition are unconfirmed.

WordStream reports 1.63% Health & Fitness CTR for traffic campaigns, not purchase campaigns. India cost sources vary and often omit sampling. They were not blended into a false precise forecast.

Objective matters: WordStream ↗

The measurement plan

C1 hypothesisDemonstrated range earns useful product interest.Track outbound CTR → landing-page views → purchases.
C2 hypothesisCustomer evidence reduces purchase hesitation.Track purchase rate and CPA. CTR alone cannot prove trust.

Hold audience, offer and destination constant. Compare actual cost and purchases. Let results choose the winner.

Proposed evaluation, not a campaign that was run. No statistical or commercial outcome is claimed.
